Members, where JustSpeak really falls on this is that we ask the committee to look at what the evidence tells us then about what does work. And we do know that stable housing works, adequate income support works, wraparound mental health services, addiction treatment, recovery services, and long-term relationship-based support, we know works.

Overseas experience and studies demonstrate that. If you had a chance to read our written submissions, a recent American study that we've cited there says that move on orders and citations fail to reduce urban disorder, but create instead a spatial churn in which homeless people circulate between neighborhoods and police jurisdictions rather than leaving public space.

And the authors of that study found that these types of approaches actually reproduce homelessness. Studies examining move on powers and criminalization of homelessness have found that people are not removed, they're simply displaced from one location to another. And so the underlying homelessness remains, the poverty that's caused that remains, and the underlying social issues also remain.

The only thing that does change is where those people are seen within our society. And so that brings me to where our real concern is about this bill, and that is the criminalization of homelessness. And a person sleeping rough, of course, is not committing homelessness, they're experiencing it. And should this bill be passed, all it does, in our view, is create another pathway into the justice system for individuals whose primary issue is issues of poverty, of housing insecurity, trauma, addiction, and disconnection.

And we know that contact with the justice system itself can be harmful for people. Further research that we've cited shows that the early engagement with the justice system increases the likelihood of re-offending and can steer people away from pro-social pathways and opportunities. And once people become involved with the justice system, it becomes harder to secure employment, housing, and their lifestyle becomes unstable.

And so for people who are already struggling, this can be another barrier that they carry for years. There are also some practical concerns that JustSpeak has. The offenses under this amendment carry a maximum penalty of three months imprisonment. And we know that once someone enters the criminal justice system, the consequences can extend far beyond the statutory maximum penalty.

So for example, those who we see regularly before the courts with long conviction histories and with difficulties with being granted bail are at risk of having remands in custody longer than the statutory maximum that they'd receive for offenses under the act. So issues of disorderly conduct, violence, intimidation, blocking public ways are already addressed within the Summary Offences Act.

So whether homelessness itself should be a trigger for police intervention, and the criminal justice involvement, we say that shouldn't be the case. So we say that as a values question, how do we deal with our most vulnerable?

Do we offer a hand up or do we encourage people to simply move somewhere else so that we can't see them?
